questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Biology?
options: The scientific study of living organisms
The study of rocks and soil layers
The measurement of forces and motion
questions.correctAnswer: The scientific study of living organisms
questions.explanation: Biology focuses on living things, their structures, functions, interactions, and environments.
questions.learningOutcome: Define Biology as the scientific study of living organisms and their interactions.

questions.prompt: Which branch of Biology mainly studies plants?
questions.correctAnswer: Botany
questions.explanation: Botany is the branch of Biology concerned with the study of plants.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate fields of study in Biology to the organisms or processes they study.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to study how fish behave in a pond ecosystem. Which field of Biology is most relevant?
questions.correctAnswer: Ecology
questions.explanation: Ecology studies how organisms interact with one another and with their environment.
questions.learningOutcome: Connect biological fields to real-life study situations.

questions.prompt: Which career most directly applies knowledge of animal health and diseases?
questions.correctAnswer: Veterinary medicine
questions.explanation: Veterinary medicine uses biological knowledge to diagnose, treat, and prevent animal diseases.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate Biology to career opportunities in health, agriculture, and conservation.

questions.prompt: A community has frequent malaria cases. Which biological knowledge is most useful in reducing the spread?
options: Life cycle and control of mosquitoes
questions.correctAnswer: Life cycle and control of mosquitoes
questions.explanation: Understanding the mosquito vector helps people remove breeding sites and reduce disease transmission.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply biological knowledge to health and environmental challenges in the community.

questions.prompt: Why is accurate observation important when studying living organisms?
options: It provides reliable evidence for biological conclusions
It replaces the need for any practical work
It makes all organisms look the same
It removes the need to record findings
questions.correctAnswer: It provides reliable evidence for biological conclusions
questions.explanation: Careful observation helps learners collect evidence that can be checked, compared, and explained.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the role of scientific skills in studying biological phenomena.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows Biology contributing to food security in Kenya?
options: Painting farm buildings with bright colours
Replacing all practical lessons with speeches
Selling farm tools without training farmers
questions.correctAnswer: Developing disease-resistant crop varieties
questions.explanation: Biological research can improve crops and livestock, increasing reliable food production.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse how Biology contributes to solving everyday problems.

questions.prompt: A class wants to show how Biology supports conservation. Which project plan is most suitable?
options: Survey plant species in the school compound and recommend ways to protect them
Copy plant names from a poster without checking the school environment
Collect as many insects as possible and discard them after class
Debate football results during the Biology lesson
questions.correctAnswer: Survey plant species in the school compound and recommend ways to protect them
questions.explanation: A survey linked to conservation uses observation, identification, and responsible action.
questions.learningOutcome: Design simple Biology-based activities that promote conservation and responsible living.

questions.prompt: Which apparatus is most suitable for collecting flying insects such as butterflies?
questions.correctAnswer: Sweep net
questions.explanation: A sweep net is used to catch small flying or grass-dwelling insects with minimal harm.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify apparatus used for collecting biological specimens.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of labelling a collected specimen?
options: To keep accurate information about where and when it was collected
questions.correctAnswer: To keep accurate information about where and when it was collected
questions.explanation: A label records useful details such as date, place, collector, and habitat for later study.
questions.learningOutcome: State the importance of labelling specimens during biological study.

questions.prompt: Which tool is most suitable for examining small features on a leaf in the field?
questions.correctAnswer: Hand lens
questions.explanation: A hand lens magnifies small structures while learners are observing specimens outdoors.
questions.learningOutcome: Select suitable tools for observing and handling biological specimens.

questions.prompt: Which practice best protects learners while collecting specimens near a school garden?
options: Wearing gloves and following the teacher's safety instructions
Touching unknown organisms with bare hands
Collecting beside a busy road without supervision
questions.correctAnswer: Wearing gloves and following the teacher's safety instructions
questions.explanation: Protective gear and supervision reduce injury, bites, contamination, and road safety risks.
questions.learningOutcome: Observe safety precautions when collecting biological specimens.

questions.prompt: Which method is used to preserve plant specimens in a herbarium?
questions.correctAnswer: Pressing, drying, mounting, and labelling
questions.explanation: Herbarium specimens are flattened, dried, mounted, and labelled for long-term reference.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe basic procedures for preserving plant specimens.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to collect small animals living in leaf litter. Which apparatus is most appropriate?
questions.correctAnswer: Tullgren funnel
questions.explanation: A Tullgren funnel drives small animals from leaf litter into a collecting container.
questions.learningOutcome: Choose apparatus for collecting specimens from different habitats.

questions.prompt: Why should learners avoid over-collecting organisms from one habitat?
options: It can reduce biodiversity and disturb the ecosystem
It makes the habitat easier to name
It increases the number of organisms left behind
It prevents the need for observation
questions.correctAnswer: It can reduce biodiversity and disturb the ecosystem
questions.explanation: Responsible collection protects populations and keeps ecological relationships stable.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain responsible and ethical practices during specimen collection.

questions.prompt: A freshly collected leaf is left in a closed plastic bag under the sun. What is the most likely problem?
options: It may wilt or decay quickly because heat and moisture encourage breakdown
It will automatically become a permanent specimen
It will produce seeds within minutes
It will turn into an animal specimen
questions.correctAnswer: It may wilt or decay quickly because heat and moisture encourage breakdown
questions.explanation: Fresh specimens should be handled quickly and properly because warm, moist conditions speed decomposition.
questions.learningOutcome: Predict effects of poor specimen handling on biological materials.

questions.prompt: Which label gives the most useful scientific record for a preserved grass specimen?
options: Grass, school field, 12 March 2026, dry open area, collected by Amina
Specimen number without place or date
questions.correctAnswer: Grass, school field, 12 March 2026, dry open area, collected by Amina
questions.explanation: A useful label includes identity, location, date, habitat, and collector details.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate specimen labels for completeness and scientific usefulness.

questions.prompt: A class has no commercial insect collecting jars. Which improvised plan is safest and most scientific?
options: Use clean transparent containers with air holes, labels, and gentle handling instructions
Use unlabelled containers and mix all organisms together
Keep insects in a closed hot bottle near a flame
Put unknown insects directly into students' pockets
questions.correctAnswer: Use clean transparent containers with air holes, labels, and gentle handling instructions
questions.explanation: Improvised apparatus should still protect learners, preserve information, and reduce harm to organisms.
questions.learningOutcome: Design safe improvised methods for collecting and preserving specimens.

questions.prompt: Which cell structure controls the activities of a eukaryotic cell?
questions.correctAnswer: Nucleus
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains genetic material that controls many cell activities.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify major cell structures and state their functions.

questions.prompt: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
questions.correctAnswer: Cell wall
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall outside the cell membrane; animal cells do not.
questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish between plant and animal cell structures.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of the cell membrane?
options: It controls movement of substances into and out of the cell
It makes the cell rigid like wood
questions.correctAnswer: It controls movement of substances into and out of the cell
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is selectively permeable, so it regulates exchange with the environment.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain functions of cell organelles and boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which organelle is the site of photosynthesis in green plant cells?
questions.correctAnswer: Chloroplast
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which traps light energy for photosynthesis.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate cell organelles to their roles in life processes.

questions.prompt: Why is iodine solution used when preparing an onion epidermis slide?
options: To stain cell structures so they are easier to see
To dissolve the cell wall completely
To make the microscope lens brighter
To kill all cells before mounting
questions.correctAnswer: To stain cell structures so they are easier to see
questions.explanation: A stain increases contrast, making parts such as the nucleus more visible under a microscope.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe steps used to prepare and observe temporary cell slides.

questions.prompt: A root hair cell has a long projection. How does this adaptation help the plant?
options: It increases surface area for water and mineral absorption
It helps the root carry out photosynthesis
It pumps blood through the plant
questions.correctAnswer: It increases surface area for water and mineral absorption
questions.explanation: The long projection provides a larger contact area with soil water and dissolved mineral ions.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate specialised cell structures to their functions.

questions.prompt: Which feature helps red blood cells transport oxygen efficiently?
options: They contain haemoglobin and have no nucleus when mature
They have large permanent vacuoles full of cell sap
questions.correctAnswer: They contain haemoglobin and have no nucleus when mature
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin binds oxygen, and the lack of a nucleus gives more space for haemoglobin.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how animal cells are specialised for specific functions.

questions.prompt: Which microscope part is first adjusted to bring a specimen into rough focus?
questions.correctAnswer: Coarse adjustment knob
questions.explanation: The coarse adjustment knob moves the stage or body tube quickly to obtain rough focus.
questions.learningOutcome: Use microscope parts appropriately when observing prepared slides.

questions.prompt: If a microscope eyepiece is x10 and the objective lens is x40, what is the total magnification?
questions.explanation: Total magnification is found by multiplying eyepiece magnification by objective magnification.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate microscope magnification from eyepiece and objective lenses.

questions.prompt: A cell has a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large permanent vacuole. What is the best conclusion?
options: It is a plant cell adapted for support and photosynthesis
It is an animal cell specialised for movement
It is a red blood cell carrying oxygen
It is a bacterium without internal structures
questions.correctAnswer: It is a plant cell adapted for support and photosynthesis
questions.explanation: The combination of a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large vacuole is typical of plant cells.
questions.learningOutcome: Infer cell type from observed cell structures.

questions.prompt: Which comparison between xylem vessels and red blood cells is accurate?
options: Both are specialised for transport, but xylem carries water while red blood cells carry oxygen
Both are living cells with large nuclei throughout life
Both move food from leaves to roots only
questions.correctAnswer: Both are specialised for transport, but xylem carries water while red blood cells carry oxygen
questions.explanation: Specialised cells and tissues have structures suited to their transport roles in plants and animals.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare specialised cells and tissues in plants and animals.

questions.prompt: A slide appears clear but the cells are almost invisible. Which improvement is most likely to help?
options: Add a suitable stain and adjust the diaphragm for contrast
Remove the coverslip and blow dust across the slide
Use the coarse adjustment at high power only
Wash the objective lens with soil water
questions.correctAnswer: Add a suitable stain and adjust the diaphragm for contrast
questions.explanation: Staining and correct light control improve contrast without damaging the microscope or specimen.
questions.learningOutcome: Troubleshoot common problems when observing cells under a microscope.

questions.prompt: Which investigation best tests whether light intensity affects chloroplast distribution in leaf cells?
options: Observe similar leaf cells kept under different light intensities and compare chloroplast positions
Taste leaves from different trees and choose the sweetest
Count stones near the plant and record their colour
Measure the mass of the microscope before and after use
questions.correctAnswer: Observe similar leaf cells kept under different light intensities and compare chloroplast positions
questions.explanation: A fair investigation changes light intensity while observing comparable cells for a measurable response.
questions.learningOutcome: Plan investigations that relate cell structure to environmental conditions.

questions.prompt: A learner is preparing a temporary slide of cheek cells. Which sequence is most suitable?
options: Place cells on a slide, add stain, lower coverslip gently, then observe
Heat the dry cells strongly, add soil, then cover with paper
Place whole cheek tissue under low power without a slide
Add oil first, crush the lens, then observe
questions.correctAnswer: Place cells on a slide, add stain, lower coverslip gently, then observe
questions.explanation: A good slide preparation protects the specimen and lens while making cells visible for observation.
questions.learningOutcome: Create safe and orderly procedures for preparing temporary cell slides.

questions.prompt: Which chemical element is found in all carbohydrates?
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are organic compounds made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify elements found in major biological molecules.

questions.prompt: Which reagent is used to test for starch in food?
questions.correctAnswer: Iodine solution
questions.explanation: Iodine solution changes from brown to blue-black when starch is present.
questions.learningOutcome: Recall standard food tests for biological molecules.

questions.prompt: What colour change indicates a positive Biuret test for proteins?
questions.correctAnswer: Blue to purple
questions.explanation: Biuret reagent turns purple in the presence of proteins.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe expected observations in food tests.

questions.prompt: Which food test requires heating with Benedict's solution?
options: Test for vitamin C by iodine
questions.correctAnswer: Test for reducing sugars
questions.explanation: Reducing sugars reduce Benedict's solution on heating, producing a green, yellow, orange, or brick-red colour.
questions.learningOutcome: Match biological food tests with their procedures.

questions.prompt: A food sample turns iodine solution blue-black. Which nutrient is present?
questions.correctAnswer: Starch
questions.explanation: The blue-black colour is the positive result for starch.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret observations from food tests.

questions.prompt: Which biological molecule is mainly used for growth and repair of body tissues?
questions.correctAnswer: Protein
questions.explanation: Proteins provide amino acids needed to build and repair tissues.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate biological molecules to their functions in organisms.

questions.prompt: Why is water important in living cells?
options: It acts as a solvent and medium for many metabolic reactions
It replaces all enzymes in reactions
It forms the cell wall in animals
questions.correctAnswer: It acts as a solvent and medium for many metabolic reactions
questions.explanation: Many cell reactions occur in water because it dissolves and transports substances.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the importance of water in cellular processes.

questions.prompt: Which result would show that a groundnut sample contains lipids using the emulsion test?
options: A milky white emulsion appears after ethanol and water are added
The sample turns iodine solution blue-black
The sample produces bubbles with limewater
The sample turns Biuret reagent purple without mixing
questions.correctAnswer: A milky white emulsion appears after ethanol and water are added
questions.explanation: Lipids dissolve in ethanol and form a cloudy white emulsion when water is added.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply correct procedures to identify lipids in food samples.

questions.prompt: A learner heats a food sample with Benedict's solution and sees an orange precipitate. What is the best interpretation?
options: Reducing sugar is present in the sample
Protein is absent because the sample was heated
questions.correctAnswer: Reducing sugar is present in the sample
questions.explanation: An orange or brick-red precipitate after heating with Benedict's solution indicates reducing sugar.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse food test observations to identify nutrients.

questions.prompt: Why should a control sample be included in a food test investigation?
options: It helps compare results and check that the test is working properly
It guarantees every sample has the same nutrient
It makes the reagent change colour before testing
It replaces the need to record observations
questions.correctAnswer: It helps compare results and check that the test is working properly
questions.explanation: A control provides a reference point for judging whether observed changes are meaningful.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate reliability in biological food test investigations.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly links a nutrient with a major function?
options: Lipids - long-term energy storage and insulation
Proteins - first source of light for photosynthesis
Water - digestion of starch by itself
questions.correctAnswer: Lipids - long-term energy storage and insulation
questions.explanation: Lipids store energy, insulate the body, and form important parts of cell membranes.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare functions of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and water.

questions.prompt: A school wants to test unknown food samples for starch, reducing sugar, protein, and lipid. Which plan is most complete?
options: Use iodine, Benedict's with heating, Biuret, and ethanol emulsion tests on separate portions
Mix all reagents into one tube and heat until dry
Taste each sample and classify it by sweetness
Use only iodine solution for every nutrient
questions.correctAnswer: Use iodine, Benedict's with heating, Biuret, and ethanol emulsion tests on separate portions
questions.explanation: Separate portions prevent interference and allow each nutrient to be tested with the proper reagent.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a systematic investigation to identify major food nutrients.

questions.prompt: What is photosynthesis?
options: The process by which green plants make food using light energy
The movement of water through xylem only
The breakdown of food to release energy in all cells
The loss of water vapour from leaves
questions.correctAnswer: The process by which green plants make food using light energy
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
questions.learningOutcome: Define photosynthesis as a plant nutrition process.

questions.prompt: Which pigment traps light energy during photosynthesis?
questions.correctAnswer: Chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light energy used to drive photosynthesis.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify structures and substances involved in photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which raw materials are required for photosynthesis?
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon dioxide and water
questions.explanation: Green plants use carbon dioxide from air and water from soil to make glucose.
questions.learningOutcome: State the raw materials needed for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which product of photosynthesis is released into the air?
questions.correctAnswer: Oxygen
questions.explanation: Oxygen is produced during photosynthesis and diffuses out of leaves.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify products of photosynthesis and their importance.

questions.prompt: Why is a destarched plant used before testing whether light is needed for photosynthesis?
options: To ensure any starch found was made during the investigation
To make the leaves permanently white
To remove all chlorophyll from the plant
To stop the plant from absorbing water
questions.correctAnswer: To ensure any starch found was made during the investigation
questions.explanation: Destarching removes stored starch so new starch production can be linked to the tested condition.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the purpose of destarching in photosynthesis experiments.

questions.prompt: In a starch test on a leaf, why is the leaf boiled in ethanol?
options: To remove chlorophyll so the iodine colour change can be seen
To add starch to the leaf
To make the leaf photosynthesise faster
questions.correctAnswer: To remove chlorophyll so the iodine colour change can be seen
questions.explanation: Ethanol removes chlorophyll, making it easier to see the blue-black colour if starch is present.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the procedure for testing leaves for starch.

questions.prompt: A variegated leaf is exposed to sunlight and tested for starch. Which area is expected to turn blue-black?
questions.correctAnswer: Only the green areas
questions.explanation: Green areas contain chlorophyll, so they photosynthesise and produce starch.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate chlorophyll distribution to starch formation in leaves.

questions.prompt: Why do plants need nitrate ions from the soil?
options: To make chlorophyll from oxygen only
To absorb light directly in roots
To change glucose into carbon dioxide
questions.correctAnswer: To make proteins for growth
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions provide nitrogen needed to build amino acids and proteins.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the role of mineral ions in plant nutrition.

questions.prompt: A plant kept in dim light grows slowly and has small pale leaves. Which factor is most likely limiting photosynthesis?
questions.correctAnswer: Light intensity
questions.explanation: Low light reduces the energy available for photosynthesis, which can slow growth.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify limiting factors of photosynthesis from observations.

questions.prompt: A leaf section covered with opaque black paper does not turn blue-black after iodine is added. What does this show?
options: Light is necessary for starch formation
Oxygen is not released by leaves
Water is made in the dark part only
questions.correctAnswer: Light is necessary for starch formation
questions.explanation: The covered part could not receive light, so it did not photosynthesise enough to form starch.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse evidence from experiments on conditions for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why magnesium deficiency causes yellowing leaves?
options: Magnesium is needed to form chlorophyll
Magnesium is the main gas used in photosynthesis
Magnesium directly becomes starch in leaves
Magnesium blocks water absorption in roots
questions.correctAnswer: Magnesium is needed to form chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Without enough magnesium, chlorophyll production falls and leaves may become yellow.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate mineral deficiencies to visible symptoms in plants.

questions.prompt: Which setup best tests whether carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis?
options: Compare a leaf in air with a similar leaf in air where carbon dioxide is absorbed by potassium hydroxide
Compare two leaves on different days without controlling light
Place one leaf in water and one in sand but change all other conditions
Cover a leaf with transparent paper and leave another uncovered
questions.correctAnswer: Compare a leaf in air with a similar leaf in air where carbon dioxide is absorbed by potassium hydroxide
questions.explanation: Removing carbon dioxide while keeping other conditions similar tests its role fairly.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate experimental designs for photosynthesis requirements.

questions.prompt: Which plant tissue mainly transports water and mineral salts?
questions.correctAnswer: Xylem
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels conduct water and dissolved mineral salts from roots to other parts of a plant.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify plant tissues involved in transport.

questions.prompt: Which plant tissue transports manufactured food from leaves to other parts?
questions.correctAnswer: Phloem
questions.explanation: Phloem transports sugars and other organic substances from sources to sinks in the plant.
questions.learningOutcome: State the role of phloem in plant transport.

questions.prompt: What is transpiration?
options: Loss of water vapour from aerial parts of a plant
Absorption of oxygen by roots only
Production of starch in the leaf
Movement of pollen from anther to stigma
questions.correctAnswer: Loss of water vapour from aerial parts of a plant
questions.explanation: Most transpiration occurs through stomata in leaves as water vapour diffuses out.
questions.learningOutcome: Define transpiration and identify where it mainly occurs.

questions.prompt: Which root hair cell feature helps absorb water from the soil?
options: Large surface area and thin cell wall
questions.correctAnswer: Large surface area and thin cell wall
questions.explanation: A root hair's shape and thin wall allow efficient contact with soil water.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain adaptations of roots for water absorption.

questions.prompt: Which condition is likely to increase the rate of transpiration?
options: Low temperature and still humid air
questions.correctAnswer: High temperature and moving air
questions.explanation: Heat increases evaporation and moving air removes water vapour around the leaf.
questions.learningOutcome: Predict how environmental factors affect transpiration rate.

questions.prompt: Why does wilting occur when a plant loses more water than it absorbs?
options: Cells lose turgor pressure and become flaccid
Cells gain too much starch and burst
questions.correctAnswer: Cells lose turgor pressure and become flaccid
questions.explanation: Water loss lowers turgor, so soft tissues droop and leaves wilt.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate water balance to support in herbaceous plants.

questions.prompt: In a potometer investigation, what does faster movement of the air bubble indicate?
options: A higher rate of water uptake by the shoot
A lower light intensity around the leaves
Food moving faster in the phloem only
questions.correctAnswer: A higher rate of water uptake by the shoot
questions.explanation: A potometer estimates transpiration by measuring water uptake, shown by air bubble movement.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret results from simple investigations on transpiration.

questions.prompt: A plant stem is placed in coloured water and the colour later appears in leaf veins. What does this demonstrate?
questions.correctAnswer: Water moves through xylem vessels
questions.explanation: Coloured water traces the pathway of water through xylem into the leaf veins.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse experimental evidence for transport pathways in plants.

questions.prompt: Which comparison between xylem and phloem is most accurate?
options: Xylem mainly carries water upward, while phloem carries manufactured food to growing or storage regions
Xylem carries glucose only downward, while phloem carries water only upward
Both carry only oxygen to the roots
questions.correctAnswer: Xylem mainly carries water upward, while phloem carries manufactured food to growing or storage regions
questions.explanation: Xylem and phloem are vascular tissues with different transport materials and directions.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare xylem and phloem transport functions.

questions.prompt: Which setup best investigates the effect of wind on transpiration using a potometer?
options: Measure bubble movement with still air, then repeat with a fan at the same distance while keeping light and temperature similar
Use two different plant species in different rooms with no measurements
Remove all leaves before placing the shoot near a fan
Change wind, light, and temperature together and record only leaf colour
questions.correctAnswer: Measure bubble movement with still air, then repeat with a fan at the same distance while keeping light and temperature similar
questions.explanation: A fair test changes wind while controlling other factors that affect transpiration.
questions.learningOutcome: Design controlled investigations on factors affecting transpiration.

questions.prompt: A crop field experiences hot dry winds. Which plant response would best reduce water loss?
options: Opening stomata wider throughout the day
Increasing leaf surface area without limits
questions.correctAnswer: Closing stomata to reduce transpiration
questions.explanation: Closing stomata reduces water vapour loss, although it may also reduce carbon dioxide intake.
questions.learningOutcome: Predict adaptive plant responses to water stress.

questions.prompt: Which farm advice best applies knowledge of transpiration to young seedlings in a dry area?
options: Water in the cooler part of the day and use mulch to reduce evaporation from soil
Water at noon only and remove all shade immediately
Cut all roots to stop water loss
Spray leaves with salt water to increase uptake
questions.correctAnswer: Water in the cooler part of the day and use mulch to reduce evaporation from soil
questions.explanation: Cooler watering and mulching conserve soil moisture and help seedlings maintain water balance.
questions.learningOutcome: Create practical water-conservation recommendations using plant transport knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which gas is used by plants during aerobic respiration?
questions.correctAnswer: Oxygen
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to release energy from glucose.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify gases involved in plant respiration.

questions.prompt: Through which structures do most gases enter and leave a leaf?
questions.correctAnswer: Stomata
questions.explanation: Stomata are pores controlled by guard cells that allow gas exchange in leaves.
questions.learningOutcome: Name structures involved in gaseous exchange in leaves.

questions.prompt: What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
options: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy
questions.correctAnswer: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen and releases energy.
questions.learningOutcome: State the word equation for aerobic respiration.

questions.prompt: Why do plant roots need oxygen from air spaces in the soil?
options: For aerobic respiration to release energy for active transport
For photosynthesis in root hair cells
questions.correctAnswer: For aerobic respiration to release energy for active transport
questions.explanation: Root cells respire to release energy used in processes such as mineral ion uptake.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain why plant organs require oxygen for respiration.

questions.prompt: During bright daylight, why may a leaf release more oxygen than it uses?
options: Photosynthesis produces oxygen faster than respiration uses it
questions.correctAnswer: Photosynthesis produces oxygen faster than respiration uses it
questions.explanation: Plants respire all the time, but photosynthesis can exceed respiration in bright light.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare photosynthesis and respiration in plants under different light conditions.

questions.prompt: A waterlogged soil has very little air. What is the most likely effect on roots?
options: Reduced respiration and poor mineral uptake
Increased oxygen supply for faster root growth
Immediate starch production in roots by photosynthesis
Formation of more stomata on root hairs
questions.correctAnswer: Reduced respiration and poor mineral uptake
questions.explanation: Waterlogging limits oxygen diffusion to roots, reducing respiration and energy supply.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse effects of oxygen shortage on plant root function.

questions.prompt: Which feature of a leaf best supports rapid gaseous exchange?
options: Large internal air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
Thick waterproof bark on the upper surface
Absence of stomata on all surfaces
Very low surface area compared with volume
questions.correctAnswer: Large internal air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
questions.explanation: Air spaces allow gases to diffuse quickly between mesophyll cells and stomata.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate leaf anatomy to gaseous exchange.

questions.prompt: Which investigation best shows that germinating seeds release carbon dioxide during respiration?
options: Place germinating seeds near limewater and observe it turning milky
Put dry sand in iodine solution and observe blue-black colour
Cover green leaves with black paper and test for starch
Place a stem in coloured water and observe leaf veins
questions.correctAnswer: Place germinating seeds near limewater and observe it turning milky
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky, so this setup gives evidence of respiration.
questions.learningOutcome: Design investigations to demonstrate products of respiration.

questions.prompt: A farmer notices seedlings die after heavy flooding. Which recommendation best uses respiration knowledge?
options: Improve drainage so oxygen can reach the roots
Keep adding more water to remove carbon dioxide
Cover the leaves with oil to stop gas exchange
Plant all seedlings deeper under wet soil
questions.correctAnswer: Improve drainage so oxygen can reach the roots
questions.explanation: Drainage restores air spaces in soil, allowing root cells to respire aerobically.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply plant respiration knowledge to crop management decisions.

questions.prompt: Which explanation best connects stomatal closure with both water conservation and gas exchange?
options: Closing stomata reduces water loss but also limits carbon dioxide entry
Closing stomata increases carbon dioxide entry and water loss
Closing stomata stops respiration in all plant cells
Closing stomata changes oxygen into glucose
questions.correctAnswer: Closing stomata reduces water loss but also limits carbon dioxide entry
questions.explanation: Stomata balance the need for carbon dioxide uptake with the risk of water loss by transpiration.
questions.learningOutcome: Evaluate trade-offs in stomatal control of plant gas exchange.

questions.prompt: Which process breaks down large food molecules into smaller soluble molecules?
questions.correctAnswer: Digestion
questions.explanation: Digestion changes large insoluble food molecules into smaller soluble molecules for absorption.
questions.learningOutcome: Define digestion as part of animal nutrition.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme begins the digestion of starch in the mouth?
questions.correctAnswer: Amylase
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase begins converting starch into simpler sugars in the mouth.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify enzymes involved in digestion of food molecules.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of villi in the small intestine?
options: They increase surface area for absorption of digested food
They grind food into smaller pieces
They produce bile to emulsify fats
They store undigested food before egestion
questions.correctAnswer: They increase surface area for absorption of digested food
questions.explanation: Villi provide a large surface area and a short diffusion distance for absorption.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain adaptations of the small intestine for absorption.

questions.prompt: Why is bile important in fat digestion?
options: It emulsifies fats into small droplets
It digests proteins into amino acids
It converts starch directly into glucose
questions.correctAnswer: It emulsifies fats into small droplets
questions.explanation: Emulsification increases the surface area of fats for lipase action.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the role of bile in digestion.

questions.prompt: A learner eats ugali, beans, and sukuma wiki. Which nutrient in beans mainly supports growth and tissue repair?
questions.correctAnswer: Protein
questions.explanation: Beans are a common source of plant protein needed for growth and repair.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate common foods to nutrients needed by the body.

questions.prompt: Which comparison between mechanical and chemical digestion is accurate?
options: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food, while chemical digestion uses enzymes
Mechanical digestion uses enzymes, while chemical digestion only chews food
Both occur only in the large intestine
Both produce oxygen for the blood
questions.correctAnswer: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food, while chemical digestion uses enzymes
questions.explanation: Chewing and churning are mechanical, while enzymes chemically break food molecules.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare types of digestion in animals.

questions.prompt: A person's diet lacks enough fibre. Which effect is most likely?
options: Constipation due to slow movement of food remains
Starch digestion stops in the mouth
questions.correctAnswer: Constipation due to slow movement of food remains
questions.explanation: Dietary fibre adds bulk and helps food remains move through the large intestine.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse the importance of balanced diet components in human health.

questions.prompt: Which school lunch choice best supports balanced nutrition for an active Grade 10 learner?
options: Ugali, beans, sukuma wiki, fruit, and clean drinking water
Plain salt with no main meal
questions.correctAnswer: Ugali, beans, sukuma wiki, fruit, and clean drinking water
questions.explanation: A balanced meal combines energy foods, body-building foods, protective foods, and water.
questions.learningOutcome: Create balanced meal choices using knowledge of nutrients.

questions.prompt: What is assimilation in animal nutrition?
options: Use of absorbed nutrients by body cells
Removal of undigested food through the anus
Movement of food by peristalsis only
questions.correctAnswer: Use of absorbed nutrients by body cells
questions.explanation: Assimilation happens when absorbed nutrients become part of cell processes and body structures.
questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish digestion, absorption, assimilation, and egestion.

questions.prompt: Which organ absorbs most water from undigested food remains?
questions.correctAnswer: Large intestine
questions.explanation: The large intestine absorbs water and mineral salts before faeces are formed.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify functions of organs in the digestive system.

questions.prompt: Which component of blood carries most oxygen?
questions.correctAnswer: Red blood cells
questions.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which carries oxygen from the lungs to body tissues.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify blood components and their transport functions.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of plasma in blood?
options: Transporting dissolved substances such as nutrients, hormones, and carbon dioxide
Breaking down starch in the mouth
questions.correctAnswer: Transporting dissolved substances such as nutrients, hormones, and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Plasma is the liquid part of blood and carries many dissolved materials around the body.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain transport roles of blood plasma.

questions.prompt: Which feature of arteries helps them withstand high blood pressure?
options: Very thin walls one cell thick
questions.correctAnswer: Thick muscular and elastic walls
questions.explanation: Arteries receive blood at high pressure, so elastic and muscular walls help them stretch and recoil.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate blood vessel structure to function.

questions.prompt: Why do veins have valves?
questions.correctAnswer: To prevent backflow of blood
questions.explanation: Valves keep blood moving toward the heart, especially where pressure is low.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain adaptations of veins for blood transport.

questions.prompt: Which blood cells are mainly involved in body defence against pathogens?
questions.correctAnswer: White blood cells
questions.explanation: White blood cells defend the body by engulfing pathogens or producing antibodies.
questions.learningOutcome: State defensive roles of blood components.

questions.prompt: What is the role of platelets in blood?
options: They help blood clot at wounds
questions.correctAnswer: They help blood clot at wounds
questions.explanation: Platelets take part in clotting, which helps prevent excessive blood loss and infection.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify roles of platelets in blood clotting.

questions.prompt: Which structure is the main site of gaseous exchange in human lungs?
questions.correctAnswer: Alveoli
questions.explanation: Alveoli provide a large, thin, moist surface for diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify structures involved in gaseous exchange in humans.

questions.prompt: During inhalation, what happens to the diaphragm?
questions.correctAnswer: It contracts and flattens
questions.explanation: When the diaphragm contracts and flattens, chest volume increases and air moves into the lungs.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe breathing movements during inhalation.

questions.prompt: Why are alveoli surrounded by many blood capillaries?
options: To maintain a steep diffusion gradient for gases
To make the lungs rigid and dry
To block oxygen from entering blood
questions.correctAnswer: To maintain a steep diffusion gradient for gases
questions.explanation: A rich blood supply quickly carries oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide, supporting diffusion.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain adaptations of alveoli for gaseous exchange.

questions.prompt: Which change occurs during vigorous exercise?
options: Breathing rate increases to supply more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide
Breathing stops because muscles make their own oxygen
The diaphragm becomes part of the digestive system
questions.correctAnswer: Breathing rate increases to supply more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Active muscles respire faster, so ventilation increases to meet gas exchange demands.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate breathing rate to energy demand during activity.

questions.prompt: Which statement best compares breathing and cellular respiration?
options: Breathing moves air into and out of lungs, while cellular respiration releases energy in cells
Breathing releases energy from glucose inside mitochondria
Cellular respiration is the movement of ribs only
Both are exactly the same process in the mouth
questions.correctAnswer: Breathing moves air into and out of lungs, while cellular respiration releases energy in cells
questions.explanation: Breathing supplies and removes gases, while cellular respiration uses oxygen to release energy from food.
questions.learningOutcome: Differentiate breathing from cellular respiration.

questions.prompt: A smoker has damaged alveolar walls, reducing surface area. What effect is most likely?
options: Less efficient gaseous exchange and lower oxygen uptake
Faster oxygen diffusion because walls are damaged
More starch production in the lungs
Complete prevention of carbon dioxide formation in cells
questions.correctAnswer: Less efficient gaseous exchange and lower oxygen uptake
questions.explanation: Reduced surface area lowers the rate of diffusion between alveoli and blood.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse how damage to gaseous exchange surfaces affects body function.
